Q: Android - How to create a responsive scrollable Column inside another Column without fixed height? A:

Use Modifier.weight(1f) on the inner Column to give it bounded height inside the parent Column.
Apply verticalScroll(rememberScrollState()) so it becomes scrollable.
Avoid fixed heights—weight keeps it responsive (or use LazyColumn for long lists).

Q: How to get the primary IP address of the local machine on Linux and OS X? A:

Using some of the other methods you may enter a conflict where multiple IP addresses is defined on the system.

This line always gets the IP address by default used.

ip route get 8.8.8.8 | head -1 | awk '{print $7}'

Here it is for IPv6

ip -6 route get 2607:f8b0:4009:802::200e | awk '{print $11}'

If you don't, you can easily get a public address to hit by using:

ping -4 google.com
ping -6 google.com

Where you replace google.com with whatever you like.

NOTE: Requires awk on your system and internet (or at a least a working DNS server on the network, or valid entry in your /etc/hosts file).

Q: Sudden change to Reverse extension method causing build errors A:

This looks to be related to a documented breaking change in C# 14 and .NET 10, namely first class span support in C# 14.

From First-class Span Types: Breaking changes: Calling Reverse on an array:

Breaking changes

As any proposal that changes conversions of existing scenarios, this proposal does introduce some new breaking changes. Here's a few examples:

Calling Reverse on an array

Calling x.Reverse() where x is an instance of type T[] would previously bind to IEnumerable<T> Enumerable.Reverse<T>(this IEnumerable<T>), whereas now it binds to void MemoryExtensions.Reverse<T>(this Span<T>). Unfortunately these APIs are incompatible (the latter does the reversal in-place and returns void).

.NET 10 mitigates this by adding an array-specific overload IEnumerable<T> Reverse<T>(this T[]), see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/107723.

void M(int[] a)
{
    foreach (var x in a.Reverse()) { } // fine previously, an error now (`Reverse` returns `void`)
    foreach (var x in Enumerable.Reverse(a)) { } // workaround
}

Design meeting: https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/main/meetings/2024/LDM-2024-09-11.md#reverse

If you building using C# 14 against the .NET 10 framework libraries the mitigation should kick in and maintain the current behavior. But in your question you note that you are using .NET 4.8 and .NET 8. In those earlier versions first-class spans had not yet been implemented, so again there should be no problem as the older enumerable overload should get bound.

However, if you are mixing C# 14 syntax with earlier framework versions or vice versa[1], then the mitigation will not kick in and you may encounter the exact compilation error you see. And in fact in comments you note:

We have a scheduled task that runs once a month to kick off a github Action that runs a build. Part of the build runs the code through a couple of vulnerability scanners (Fortify and Sonatype). Both of those run as steps after the initial build though, so they're not likely to be causing issues. Oh, and .NET SDK is 10.0.103 although the project in question is .NET 8 and .NET 4.8. It's a unit test project if that matters.

Given that the unit test project is using .NET 10 then the combination of .NET 10 based scanning tools with a .NET 8 main project could be the cause of the compilation error.

Alternatively, as suggested by Ivan Petrov and Jon Skeet, you may have set <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion> in some of your .csproj files, e.g. like so:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>  <!-- Setting this manually causes the compilation error when build using a .NET 10 tool chain -->
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
    <RootNamespace>Test</RootNamespace>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

Doing so will result in the error CS0023: Operator '.' cannot be applied to operand of type 'void' when built with a .NET 10 tool chain.

Regardless of how exactly how you you managed to mix .NET 8 with C# 14, to resolve the compilation error you should use consistent .NET and C# versions across all your projects -- in both your main project(s) and your unit test project. I.e. either make your unit testing project use .NET 8 or transition all of your projects to .NET 10. When you do, be sure not to mix earlier .NET versions with "future" C# versions.

And if you have <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion> set in some of your csproj files you should remove this, Microsoft's documentation explicitly warns not to use this setting as it can cause machine-specific build failures:

Warning

Don't set the LangVersion element to latest. The latest setting means the installed compiler uses its latest version. The value of latest can change from machine to machine, making builds unreliable. In addition, it enables language features that might require runtime or library features not included in the current SDK.

(In fact, their warning seems to precisely match the problem you are seeing.)

[1] C# 14 with .NET 8 is explicitly an unsupported combination:

C# 14 is supported only on .NET 10 and newer versions.

Q: How to use MAP() , BYCOL() or BYROW() to return multiple arrays? A:

Apply below formula in cell G1:

=LET(
 srt, SORT(TOCOL(B2:E6, 1)),
ifna, IFNA(--TRANSPOSE(TEXTSPLIT(TEXTJOIN(";",, DROP(GROUPBY(INT(srt * 10), srt, ARRAYTOTEXT,, 0),, 1)), ", ", ";")), ""),
      VSTACK(HSTACK("Items", SEQUENCE(, COLUMNS(ifna))), HSTACK(SEQUENCE(ROWS(ifna)), ifna))
)

Q: Google Apps Script HTML scriptlets trucates JSON object containing a single quote and a URL when using force-printing scriptlets A:

The problem is the apostrophe / single stright quote character in

const closingParagraphTag = `</p>`; // '

Remove it and the problem is solved.

If you think that this is a bug, please report it to Google using the issue tracker. For details see https://developers.google.com/apps-script/support
